passage:
Age two: at the crèche, Lavanya toddled over to a boy who was crying by the shoe rack. She patted his back with a flat little hand, then fetched her floppy rabbit and pushed it into his arms. The carer smiled. 'That was kind, Lavanya.'

Age nine: Sharmila noticed the new girl eating alone on the low wall for the third day. She carried her tiffin over and sat down. 'Want to share my paratha?' The girl shrugged, then nodded. When an older boy shoved the girl's bag off the wall at break, Sharmila helped pick it up and went straight to the teacher on duty to say what had happened.

Age twenty-five: Keerthana had moved to another city for her first job. Every evening she rang her mother for ten minutes, even when there was little to say, and sent a photo of her dinner. On Sundays she video-called her old college friends. The phone screen made her miss the smell of home, but she noticed the small daily calls kept the distance from feeling too wide.

qa.q: What did Lavanya give the crying boy?
qa.a: Her floppy rabbit.

qa.q: How did care look different at two, nine and twenty-five?
qa.a: Lavanya patted a crying boy's back and gave him her rabbit. Sharmila sat with the lonely new girl, shared her paratha and went to the teacher when an older boy shoved the bag, and Keerthana kept close to her mother and friends through daily calls and Sunday video calls from another city.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she looked at the phone screen?
qa.a: She missed home, yet felt reassured that the small daily calls kept the distance from feeling too wide.

qa.q: Why was going to the teacher a sensible step for Sharmila?
qa.a: The shove was unfair and could turn unsafe, so telling the adult on duty handled it properly, and Sharmila still showed care by helping with the bag first.

grounding: Care and closeness at two, nine and twenty-five: comforting a crying child, sitting with a lonely classmate, and staying in touch from far away.

passage:
At ten, Disha's best friend moved to another city. At school Disha kept her face still until the last bell, then went into the empty corridor, crouched by the wall and let the tears come. She breathed out slowly, five times, the way her class teacher had shown them. That evening she told her mother Nandini, 'I miss her so much it hurts here.' Nandini held her and said, 'Of course you do. Let's write her a letter tonight.'

At twenty, Disha was in a hostel two states away when the call came about her grandfather. She went to lectures the next day and told everyone she was fine. Her roommate Uma noticed the untouched tea. 'You don't have to be fine,' Uma said. That night Disha lit a small lamp in the room, said his name quietly and cried. She phoned her aunt, and the next week she booked a time with the college counsellor, because the heaviness had not lifted.

qa.q: What did Nandini suggest after Disha said she missed her friend?
qa.a: To write her a letter that night.

qa.q: How did Disha handle sadness at ten compared with twenty?
qa.a: At ten she cried in the empty corridor, breathed out slowly and told her mother. At twenty she first hid behind being fine far from home, then lit a lamp for her grandfather, cried, phoned her aunt and booked a time with the college counsellor.

qa.q: What was Disha likely feeling when she told everyone she was fine?
qa.a: Grief she was trying to cover, as the untouched tea shows, and probably some isolation so far from home.

qa.q: What could Uma do next to support Disha?
qa.a: Stay close, keep listening, and encourage her to keep talking with her aunt and the counsellor.

grounding: One person's way of coping with sadness at ten, crying privately and telling a parent, and at twenty, grieving far from home and reaching out.

passage:
At sixteen, Kalyani found her friend Deepika crying on the stairs. Her first thought was that someone had upset her. Instead of guessing, she sat down. 'I'm here. Do you want to tell me, or shall I just stay?' Deepika wiped her face and laughed. 'I got the lead in the play. I can't stop crying.' They stayed there until the bell.

At twenty, Kalyani sat on the hostel committee when a laptop charger went missing. The warden asked Farida, a first-year, where she had been on Friday. Farida's face went red, her hands shook, and sweat shone on her forehead. Someone at the table whispered, 'Look how nervous she is.' Kalyani shook her head slightly. 'Anyone would shake in this room,' she said. 'Let's ask the questions and check the facts, like who was in the corridor and when the charger was last seen.' Later the charger turned up in the common room, and the committee agreed that a nervous body proved nothing.

qa.q: What was the reason for Deepika's tears?
qa.a: She got the lead in the play and could not stop crying.

qa.q: How do Kalyani's two experiences show that a visible reaction can have many causes?
qa.a: Deepika's tears came from joy about the play, not the upset Kalyani first guessed. Farida's red face, shaking hands and sweat came from nerves in the warden's room, so neither showed what a quick guess would say.

qa.q: What was Farida probably feeling in the warden's room?
qa.a: Nervous and afraid of being blamed, shown by her red face, shaking hands and sweat, which were not proof of anything.

qa.q: What could the committee do instead of reading Farida's body?
qa.a: Ask clear questions, check facts such as who was in the corridor and when the charger was last seen, and treat nervousness as normal.

grounding: Tears at sixteen and sweat, blushing and trembling at twenty each have several possible causes and are not proof of feeling or guilt.

passage:
At fifteen, Gurleen walked into school and felt eyes slide away from her. A girl on the stairs stopped talking as she passed. At lunch her friend Rehana showed her a screenshot: a story that Gurleen had cheated on the maths test. Her face burned. All afternoon she counted glances, kept her head down and wished the floor would open. She could not tell who had started it. Rehana sat with her. 'I know it's false. Let's tell our maths teacher together, today.'

At twenty-five, Gurleen was walking to the pantry when she heard her name. 'She only got the promotion because...' The voices dropped. Back at her desk she felt exposed. For a week she over-polished every email, arrived early and laughed too brightly. Her colleague Farhan noticed and asked over tea if she was all right. She told him what she had overheard. 'That says more about them than about your work,' he said. 'Your last three reports speak for themselves.' She let out a long breath and sent the next email without a third rewrite.

qa.q: What false story spread about Gurleen at fifteen?
qa.a: That she had cheated on the maths test.

qa.q: What did being the subject of talk feel like for Gurleen at fifteen and at twenty-five?
qa.a: At fifteen she burned with shame and counted glances, unable to tell who had started the story. At twenty-five, hearing colleagues speak about her promotion, she felt exposed and over-polished every email.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen over-polish every email for a week?
qa.a: She felt exposed after overhearing the talk and worried about how she looked to others, so she tried hard to manage the impression.

qa.q: What could Gurleen do when she next overhears talk about herself?
qa.a: Speak to a trusted colleague like Farhan, let her steady work speak for itself, and stop rewriting to manage impressions.

grounding: One person as the subject of a false story at fifteen and of office talk at twenty-five, feeling exposed and over-managing image.

passage:
At fifteen, Mahima snapped at her father Thomas as he tapped at his laptop. 'Do you even care what happened at school today?' Thomas closed the lid. He did not answer with a list of proofs. 'It sounds like today was awful and you wanted me to notice,' he said. 'Tell me.' Mahima's shoulders dropped, and out came the story of being left out of a group photo.

At twenty-six, Mahima worked with a supplier whose team never said no plainly. She needed to know whether they could deliver early, but asking straight out had brought only 'We will see' and a pause on the call. Kalyani, a colleague who knew the supplier's manager, suggested another way. Mahima wrote a soft note: 'If early delivery is difficult, we are also happy with the original date.' She asked Kalyani to mention it over lunch. The reply came back through Kalyani: 'They would prefer the original date.' Mahima thanked them and changed the schedule, with no blame on either side.

qa.q: What did Thomas do when Mahima asked whether he even cared?
qa.a: He closed the lid of his laptop and said it sounded like today was awful and she wanted him to notice.

qa.q: How is asking handled differently in the two scenes, and what do they share?
qa.a: At fifteen the question was a hurt hint, so Thomas answered the feeling behind it. At twenty-six the supplier's team never said no plainly, so Mahima sent a soft note through Kalyani, and in both scenes reading the style behind the words worked better than the literal words.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she said, 'Do you even care'?
qa.a: Hurt at being left out of a group photo and wanting her father's attention, not curiosity about the answer.

qa.q: What could Mahima try when a straight question gets only 'We will see'?
qa.a: Offer an easy way out for the other side, such as a soft note through a trusted colleague, and watch for softeners and silence that mean no.

grounding: A rhetorical question at fifteen and an indirect-style question at twenty-six show that asking is shaped by feeling and culture.

passage:
Age five: Vidya announced, 'I am the doctor,' and hung a paper-cup stethoscope around her neck. Her cousins soon wanted to switch to a train game. Vidya crossed her arms. 'I said doctor,' she said, even though the dolls she was examining had long been forgotten and nobody else was playing.

Age ten: Vishal boasted to his classmates that the gold ribbon at sports day would be his. Every morning he ran round the block before school. When it rained, he ran under the awnings of the shops instead, and when his legs ached he still went out, because he had said it aloud in front of everyone. On the day he finished second and his ears burned, yet he had never skipped one practice.

Age twenty: Raghav sat at the back of a course he found dull. He had paid for the whole year, spent six months on it and told all his friends and relatives about it at Diwali. In his hostel room he opened a job listing that fitted him better and closed it again. Quitting, he thought, would feel like saying he had been wrong. He packed his bag for the next lecture, and the listing stayed in a tab.

qa.q: How did Vishal keep up his practice when it rained?
qa.a: He ran under the awnings of the shops instead.

qa.q: What is common in how Vidya, Vishal and Raghav stick to what they said?
qa.a: Each keeps to a spoken word. Vidya stays in the doctor game though nobody is playing, Vishal runs every morning after boasting, and Raghav stays in a dull course because he paid and told his friends. The word helped Vishal's effort but held Vidya and Raghav in things that no longer worked.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he closed the job listing?
qa.a: Torn: he was drawn to a better fit but felt that quitting would mean admitting he had been wrong.

qa.q: What could Raghav do to weigh his choice more fairly?
qa.a: Ask whether he would choose the course today if he had not already paid, and talk it over with an adviser or a trusted friend.

grounding: Sticking to a spoken word at five, ten and twenty: stubbornness in play, effort after a public boast, and staying in a costly course.
